opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, we're quite open to it, and I'd encourage people to send those proposals. The list we publish isn't meant to be exhaustive. It's a snapshot of where we currently think there's a lot of leverage: areas where we have some idea of what success looks like and where we think additional people or funding would move things. But we're very aware that we could be wrong about the map. Some of the most important ideas in alignment probably haven't been articulated yet, and if we only funded things that matched our existing categories, we'd systematically miss them.

So the way I think about an off-list proposal is to ask the same questions I'd ask of anything else, just a bit more carefully. First, what's the theory of change? If this research works out, how does it actually make it more likely that we can deploy very capable systems safely? I'm fairly demanding about that link. There's a lot of interesting theory that's adjacent to alignment but doesn't clearly cash out in reducing risk, and that's fine work, but it's not what we're trying to fund.

Second, is there a plausible path to a crisp result? Theoretical work is valuable partly because it can give you guarantees, or at least sharp statements about when something does or doesn't work. Debate is a good example from my own history. The interesting part wasn't just "let's have models argue." It was being able to say something precise about the complexity-theoretic power of the protocol and then ask where that breaks in practice. I like proposals that have that flavour: a clear formal question whose answer would actually change what we do.

Third, why this person or team? A lot of the time, the strongest off-list proposals come from people with deep expertise in some other field, like complexity theory, cryptography, game theory, learning theory, or economics, who see a connection the alignment community has missed. That's exactly the kind of cross-pollination we want, and those people often won't frame things in our vocabulary, so I try not to penalise that.

The thing I'd caution against is relabelling. If a proposal is really just existing work in another area with "alignment" attached, that's usually pretty visible. But if someone can tell a convincing story about why their question matters for safety, I'd much rather have that conversation than have them squeeze it into one of our boxes. And if it's compelling enough, it may well end up on the next version of the list.

r001.rationale: The response welcomes off-list proposals and discusses evaluating the person or team, but it does not state that only modest confidence in the researcher is required.

r002.rationale: The response says the research list is not exhaustive and encourages cross-pollination, but it does not describe spreading chances across more approaches than current AI labs do.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm pretty open to it, honestly. The list we put out is a snapshot of what we think is tractable and important right now, given the people we have and the things we've been able to make progress on. It's not meant to be a claim that everything off the list is wrong or useless. If anything, I'd be a bit worried if people treated it as exhaustive, because the field is young enough that we're almost certainly missing things.

So when someone comes to me with a proposal that's outside the list, the questions I tend to ask are fairly simple. First, is there a story for how this connects to the actual problem? Lots of theoretical work is interesting in itself, but the thing I care about is whether, if you succeeded, you'd be able to say something concrete about whether a particular system is safe or how to make it safer. That doesn't have to be an immediate payoff. Debate, for instance, started as a fairly abstract idea about how to get humans to judge things they can't directly check, and it's taken years to get it to the point where it says anything about real models. But there was always a path, even if a long one.

Second, is there a way to tell if it's working? With theory, the failure mode is that you can go a long time generating plausible-sounding results that don't actually constrain anything. I like proposals that have some notion of what would count as a negative result, either a mathematical obstruction or an experiment that could embarrass the idea. If the only possible outcome is "this is still interesting," that's a warning sign.

And third, is the person well-placed to do it? That sounds obvious, but a lot of my job is matching people to problems. Someone with a strong background in, say, complexity theory or cryptography will often see angles on these questions that we don't, and I'd much rather they pursue that than try to force themselves into our framing.

If the answer to those is reasonably positive, I'm generally in favour, even if I'm personally sceptical of the specific direction. I've been wrong about what turns out to be useful before, and the cost of someone spending a year on a theoretical direction that doesn't pan out is low relative to the cost of the field converging too early on a narrow set of ideas. What I do push back on is work that's disconnected on all three counts, where there's no link to safety, no way to be wrong, and no particular reason this person is the one to do it. That usually isn't research, it's just a nice idea, and nice ideas are cheap.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether the proposer is well-placed to do the work and says reasonably positive answers are enough for support, but it does not state that only modest confidence in the researcher is required.

r002.rationale: The response favors exploring a broader range of ideas to avoid premature convergence, but does not describe the organisation’s portfolio as spreading chances of success more widely than current AI labs do.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t treat our current list as exhaustive. It reflects the directions we’ve identified and think we can make progress on, rather than a claim that everything else is unimportant.

For a proposal outside that list, I’d want to understand the connection to alignment: if you solved this theoretical problem, what would that let us do, or what uncertainty would it resolve? You don’t need to have the whole path worked out in advance—that would be an unreasonable requirement for research—but there should be some account of why the question matters.

Then I’d look for a concrete starting point. What’s the simplest setting in which you can investigate the idea, and what could you learn from it? I’m quite open to someone making the case for a direction we haven’t considered. The important thing is the case for the research, rather than whether it already appears on our list.

r001.rationale: The response asks for an account of why the research matters and a concrete starting point, but says nothing about how much confidence is required in the researcher proposing it.

r002.rationale: The response says the current list is not exhaustive, but does not describe the portfolio as spreading chances of success across more approaches than current AI labs.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t treat our list as exhaustive. It’s a list of directions that we currently think are promising, given our particular views and the work we’re set up to do. There could easily be important ideas outside it.

But I would want to understand the connection to the actual alignment problem. What is the obstacle you’re trying to address? If you solved the theoretical problem, what would that let us do? And what assumptions would have to hold for that result to be useful?

With theoretical work, there’s a risk that you pick a problem because it’s mathematically interesting and tractable, and then the connection to aligning a powerful system becomes quite tenuous. That doesn’t mean you should only work on things with an immediate application. It means you should keep checking that connection, and be willing to change the question if the assumptions turn out to be wrong.

So I’d be interested in a compelling argument for a new direction. Being outside the list isn’t itself an objection; the important thing is whether there’s a plausible story for how progress on it helps.

r001.rationale: The candidate asks for a compelling argument connecting a direction to alignment, but says nothing about how much confidence is needed in the researcher proposing it.
